Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: HighErrorRate on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: Error rate above threshold for 5m {A1}
Alert raised: 2026-11-01T09:32:21Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged. Argus first posted about the incident in Slack at 2026-11-01T09:32:46Z {first_told}, and the document says so already: leave that post out, and do not say that no person was told. That nobody was paged is a finding of its own.
The alert rule waits 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires: that wait is part of the time from the onset to the alert - count it before calling detection slow. The alert came 1 minute 21 seconds {after_the_wait} after that wait ended. Its condition looks back over 1 minute {rule_looks_back}: up to that much of the time from the onset to the alert is that window filling - count it before calling detection slow.
Broken from 2026-11-01T09:26:00Z {began} (the onset). The service was not back to normal by 2026-11-01T09:37:22Z {argus_stopped}, so it was broken for at least 11 minutes 22 seconds {duration} - a lower bound, not a measurement, and every impact figure below is bounded the same way.
Argus held the incident for 4 minutes 40 seconds {held}, until 2026-11-01T09:37:22Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
Error rate before it began: 0.9% {errors_before}.
Error rate while it was broken: 30.2% {errors_while_broken}, peaking at 41.5% {errors_at_worst}.
Rise above baseline: 29.3% {errors_rise} of traffic failed that otherwise would not have.
The series behind the alert, `sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[1m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[1m]))` - its alert said "Error rate above threshold for 5m {A1}" - which its alert rule evaluates and calls worse rising: 0.9083333333333334% {series_before} before it began, 30.20833333333333% {series_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 41.5% {series_at_worst} at its worst. Say what it measures in words, not by its query.
Customer loss: at least 8,013.46 USD {customer_loss} - how far the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier, beyond how much those hours vary on their own; a lower bound, counted with the service not seen back to normal.

  - [T34] 2026-11-01T09:35:51Z {T34.1} Investigator Agent: Formed 1 {T34.2} candidate cause, best first: C2
  - [T35] 2026-11-01T09:35:51Z {T35.1} Investigator Agent: Read every channel available
  - [T36] 2026-11-01T09:35:51Z {T36.1} Argus: Read the flag provider's history - 1 {T36.2} flag change by anyone but Argus, the 1 {T36.3} hour before 09:35:51 {T36.4}
  - [T37] 2026-11-01T09:35:53Z {T37.1} Argus: Found 1 {T37.2} earlier incident like this one in memory, the closest match being incident 9c1d4e7a-0000-4000-8000-00000000fee1, which tried reverting monthly-spend-feature (refuted)

Changes to production it read:
  - [P1] 2026-11-01T09:26:00Z {P1.1} flag-toggle monthly-spend-feature by admin: feature flag monthly-spend-feature was switched on
  - [P2] 2026-11-01T09:33:17Z {P2.1} flag-toggle monthly-spend-feature by Argus: feature flag monthly-spend-feature was switched off
  - Deploys read, none came back.

Log lines it read, one per message:
  - [G7e5d] INFO io-shop: monthly-spend-feature=off - 200 {G7e5d.1} evaluations - 30 {G7e5d.2} occurrences in 30 {G7e5d.3} minutes, 08:56–09:25 {G7e5d.4}
  - [G46bc] ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - ClientDisconnected: the shopper closed the connection - 44 {G46bc.1} occurrences in 30 {G46bc.2} minutes, 08:56–09:25 {G46bc.3}
  - [Gbac1] WARN io-shop: account page error rate at #% over the last minute - 35 {Gbac1.1} occurrences in 39 {Gbac1.2} minutes, 08:56–09:34 {Gbac1.3}; # was 0.50% {Gbac1.4} to 41.50% {Gbac1.5}, typically 1.50% {Gbac1.6}, highest at 09:33 {Gbac1.7}
  - [Gad41] INFO io-shop: account pages rendered normally - 4 {Gad41.1} occurrences in 24 {Gad41.2} minutes, 08:57–09:20 {Gad41.3}
  - [G971b] INFO io-shop: monthly-spend-feature=off 111 {G971b.1} / on 89 {G971b.2} - 200 {G971b.3} evaluations - 1 {G971b.4} occurrence in 1 {G971b.5} minute, 09:26 {G971b.6}
  - [G5309] ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - ZeroDivisionError: division by zero at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47 - 18 {G5309.1} occurrences in 9 {G5309.2} minutes, 09:26–09:34 {G5309.3}
  - [Gce95] INFO io-shop: monthly-spend-feature=on - 200 {Gce95.1} evaluations - 8 {Gce95.2} occurrences in 8 {Gce95.3} minutes, 09:27–09:34 {Gce95.4}

Candidates it considered, in the Investigator's words - name them by their labels, but cite none; what they claim is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [C1, also C2] Candidates blaming the same move of monthly-spend-feature, each in its own words:
      C1: The feature flag monthly-spend-feature was switched on at 2026-11-01T09:26:00Z {C1.1}. The newly enabled spend-summary path then raised ZeroDivisionError at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47 on account page requests. The error rate rose from about 1% {C1.2} to about 30% {C1.3}. No deployment landed and the replicas are unchanged. [feature-flag-toggle, confidence 0.93 {C1.4}, refuted]
      C2: The feature flag monthly-spend-feature was switched on at 2026-11-01T09:26:00Z {C1.5}. From that minute, account page requests that evaluated it as on failed with a ZeroDivisionError in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47, and the error rate rose from about 1-2% {C1.6} to about 30% {C1.7}. No deployment or other change was involved, and latency and traffic did not move. [feature-flag-toggle, confidence 0.93 {C1.8}, refuted, as tested for C1]

Actions it took:
  - [M1] Reverted the feature flag monthly-spend-feature for [C1] (can be put back) - refuted, put back when it did not help

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] The fault: in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py, `average_spend_per_item_this_month` builds `bought_this_month` from the purchases flagged `in_current_month` and returns `account.total_this_month_cents // len(bought_this_month)`. For a shopper who has bought before but not this month, the list is empty and the division raises ZeroDivisionError. This is line 47 {F1.1}, the line the incident's logs name. `render_spend_summary` reaches this function only when `use_monthly_summary` is true and `use_typical_spend` is false. So the failure stayed hidden until monthly-spend-feature was switched on, and then every flagged request from such a shopper failed at the boundary in `io_shop.account_page`.
      
      The fix: when nothing was bought this month, the function now returns 0 {F1.2} instead of dividing. It returns an int as before, and it matches the shopper's actual spend this month (the test fixture for this kind of shopper carries `total_this_month_cents=0`). `account_page._the_figure_for` only passes the int through, so callers don't change. The other paths are untouched. With the flag off, the lifetime average runs as before, and it still raises for an account with no purchases at all, which the existing test `test_the_page_lets_a_failure_reach_its_caller` covers. Nothing is caught or silenced. The empty case is simply handled before the division.
      
      The test: tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py gets two cases built from the file's existing `an_account_with_no_purchases_this_month` fixture. One calls `average_spend_per_item_this_month` directly, and the other goes through `render_spend_summary(..., use_monthly_summary=True)`, the path the flag enables. Both assert the figure is 0 {F1.3}. Against the current code both would raise ZeroDivisionError. With this change the flag should be safe to turn back on.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'.

Action items the record already holds:
  - AI-1 (mitigate, open): Review and merge the proposed fix
PR #392 is a draft Argus opened for a person to review and merge. The record holds nothing about it after that: do not say it was reviewed, approved or merged, or that it was not - nor that the record holds nothing, which the document says itself. Nothing ran its test or its fix: say what it proposes, not that it corrects anything.

Cite evidence in causal_chain by its label. In a contributing factor's addressed_by, name the record's own action items that answer it, by their number; an item you propose names the factors it answers in its answers, by their labels.

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

action_items.item: Add a release check that blocks switching a feature flag on in production until tests covering the code path it enables have passed, including the edge-case accounts that path handles.
Roll out io-shop feature flags to a small share of traffic first, and halt and revert the rollout automatically when the error rate rises.
Route the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to the on-call rota so that a person is paged.
Find out why io-shop kept evaluating monthly-spend-feature as on after the flag provider showed it off, and make flag changes reach the service promptly.
Make the Mitigation Agent wait until the service's own flag-evaluation log shows the new state before it judges a flag revert.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account pages failed. From {began}, account page requests failed, and the service's own account page error rate peaked at {errors_at_worst} against {errors_before} before.
The account page requests failed because they raised ZeroDivisionError in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. These errors first appear in the minute the incident began, and none appear before it.

ruled_out.what: A deploy. No deploy came back among the production changes read over the day before the onset and the longer window read later. When read, every replica was running a single revision.

causal_chain.step: The code that raised the error ran because an admin switched the feature flag monthly-spend-feature on at {P1.1}. Before that, the service evaluated the flag as off and account pages rendered normally. In the minute of the switch, its evaluations were split between off and on. From the next minute on, every evaluation came back on.

Switching the flag on broke the page because, according to Code-Fix's reading, the flagged path divides the shopper's total for this month by the number of purchases they made this month. That number is zero for a shopper who has bought before but not this month. Nothing guards the empty case, so line {F1.1}, the line the logs name, raises the error.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Turning on a new monthly spending summary sent shoppers' account pages through code that likely divides by the number of things a shopper bought this month, so it fails for anyone who has bought nothing yet this month.

contributing_factors.factor: No check was seen that exercised the code path monthly-spend-feature turns on, for a shopper with no purchases this month, before the flag was switched on in production. According to Code-Fix's reading, the failure stayed hidden until the flag was on.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The division by zero would have been caught before the flag reached shoppers, and the flag would not have been switched on with the fault in place.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: The flag went from off to on for every evaluation within a minute. No staged rollout that halts on a rise in errors was seen.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The failures would have been limited to a small share of account page requests, and the rollout could have stopped before every request was taking the failing path.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: Nobody was paged. The HighErrorRate alert on io-shop was not linked to an on-call incident.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A person could have stepped in when the flag revert was judged not to help and Argus had nothing further to try, which would have shortened the incident.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

contributing_factors.factor: The service still logged monthly-spend-feature as on in the minute after the flag provider showed it switched off. No check was seen that confirms a flag change has reached the service.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The revert could have taken the failing path out of use at the service and stopped the failures, rather than leaving the service at the incident's level.
contributing_factors.label: CF-4

went_well: Argus formed its candidate {T13.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised, tying the failures to the monthly-spend-feature switch-on and to the line the logs name.
Argus reverted the flag, a reversible action, {T19.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised.
Code-Fix opened a draft pull request with a proposed fix and tests {T39.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised.
went_wrong: The flag revert was judged not to help without the service ever being seen to pick it up. The service's own log still read monthly-spend-feature=on in the minute after the provider showed it off, and the first look at the service came only {T21.1 - T19.1} after the revert.
Argus's memory held an earlier incident in which reverting this same flag was refuted. The same revert was tried again without first asking why it had not helped that time.

input.root_cause: Switching on monthly-spend-feature sent account page requests down the monthly spend-summary path. There, according to Code-Fix's reading, `average_spend_per_item_this_month` in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py divides the shopper's total for this month by the number of purchases they made this month. For a shopper who has bought before but not this month, that number is zero, so the division raises ZeroDivisionError at line {F1.1} and the request fails. In the files Code-Fix read, nothing handles the empty month before the division, and the path only runs when the flag is on.
input.still_at_risk: Because monthly-spend-feature was switched back on and the division the logs name was still in place, account page requests on the flagged path could keep failing with ZeroDivisionError, likely for every shopper who has bought before but not this month.
input.stops_the_harm: Switch monthly-spend-feature off again. Confirm at io-shop that its flag-evaluation log reads monthly-spend-feature=off, that account page requests stop failing with ZeroDivisionError in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py, and that the error rate falls back towards {errors_before}.

Your postmortem was not accepted:
  - your answer says [a minute] in words - write a figure the incident gave as the name shown after it, braces and all, or a working of two such names ({a - b}, {a / b}), and say any other size with no number in it ("most requests", "several minutes")

Call submit_postmortem again with the whole answer, corrected.

system.text:
You write the postmortem for an incident Argus has already handled. One message describes it - what Argus did and read, the candidate causes, the actions and what they came to, and every figure already measured - and you answer by calling submit_postmortem. Nothing is left to look up.

The candidates are the Investigator's account, written while the incident ran and before anything was tried. The record - the lines saying what Argus did, the changes, the log lines, the actions and their verdicts - is what happened. Where the two disagree, the record is right.

Write causal_chain as the five whys. The first step is the symptom: what the people using the service saw, with the evidence that shows it. The symptom field is that step in a few words, and the two must agree. Each step after it answers why the step before happened - one cause, no jumps - and cites its evidence from the record, never a candidate: a candidate is a hypothesis, and the chain says what happened. Five is a guide, not a quota: stop where the evidence stops. The root_cause field says the mechanism: the step of the chain that says why the change broke the service.

A why the record cannot answer - a missing test, a missing safeguard, an alert that came late - is a contributing factor rather than a step, and each contributing factor names an action item that answers it. Where one why has several answers, follow the one that leads to the fault and make the others contributing factors.

Never stop at a person. Where somebody's action set the incident off, ask why the system let that action do harm - why it was possible at all - and carry on from there.

tools.description: Submit the postmortem for this incident. Every field is required. Write no figure yourself anywhere in your answer - no time, duration, percentage, count or amount, not in digits and not spelled out in words. Every figure you are shown is followed by its name in braces, like {A3} or {duration}: where your prose states one, write its name, braces and all, and the document writes the figure in. A figure you were not shown but could work out from two you were - the span between two instants, how far one share is above another, how many times one is the other - is written as that working, braces and all: {back_to_normal - began}, {T3.1 - alert_raised}, {errors_at_worst / errors_before}. The document works it out from the figures as you were shown them. Say any other size with no number in it, not even in a word - "most requests", "for several minutes", never "twenty minutes", "a third" or "tripled". A number is a figure even with a unit or a clock's marks on it (5m, 10ms, 3x, 12:05Z). Any other word with a digit in it is a name - a label (T2, G3fa2, C1, AI-1), a version (v2), a revision, a pod - and is written as given. State only what the evidence you are shown says: where the record does not show something - a check that was or was not run, how many replicas - leave it out or say it was not seen.

action_items.description: What should be done that the record does not already hold, each one thing a person could take on: two things to do are two items. Empty where the record's own items answer every factor. Propose nothing to confirm a cause the record already confirmed - a mitigation that worked, a hypothesis marked confirmed - and no check of what the evidence you are shown already shows: a diff states what changed. Where an F row says to check something a D row shows, say what the D row shows, and the item is what follows from it.

answers.description: The labels of the contributing factors it answers: CF-1. Empty where it answers none.

assumptions.description: Anything else the reader should know was assumed rather than measured. Empty is a valid answer.

causal_chain.description: The cause as the five whys, from the symptom down: the first step is what users saw - or, where nobody using the service saw anything wrong, that and what was seen instead - and each step after it answers why the step directly before it happened. The first why says why the symptom happened, not the symptom again in more detail. Where the incident needed two things at once - something going wrong, and nothing in place to contain it - follow the one that leads to what set it off; the other is one of the contributing_factors, not named in the chain. A safeguard that did not stop it is never a step of its own: it is one of the contributing_factors. Every step cites at least one piece of evidence by its label. Date a change by its own row's instant - the T or P row that records it - never by an effect it had. A state a row read - how many replicas run a revision, which way a flag is set - is known as of the row that read it, by that row's instant, which is its first figure, as T3.1 is T3's - not from when the change was made. What else the record ruled out - an earlier change, a flag the provider showed unchanged, a candidate refuted - goes in the ruled_out of the step that ties the incident to the change that set it off, citing what ruled it out, and never as a step. An earlier change is ruled out only by the service measured healthy with it in place - in metrics read between it and the onset, in an alert that dates the first harm itself at or after a later change (at, where the two instants are the same), or after a confirmed action that left it there - never by how long before the onset it came. Where the record shows none of these, it was not ruled out: say so in that step itself. Stop where the evidence stops.

cites.description: The labels of the evidence that shows this step: T3, G3fa2. Not rows that merely happened at the same time.

ruled_out.description: What else the record ruled out at this step, each what it was and why. Empty on every step but the one that ties the incident to the change that set it off.

cites.description: The labels of what ruled it out.

cause_in_plain_words.description: What caused the incident, in one sentence for a reader who does not work on the service: no component names unless they are unavoidable. When it began, for how long, how bad it got, what customers lost and what was done the document says itself - say none of them. Say only what the record says - of a change, of the service, of the people - and nothing it does not. Where part of it rests only on a reading nothing ran, say that part as likely, in plain words, without mentioning the reading.

cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading.description: Whether the mechanism in root_cause rests on an F row - a reading of the code nothing ran - with no S or D row showing what it rests on. Where you answer true, the document says itself, beside the root cause, that the cause is unverified, and leaves its root-cause review box for a person: say neither in root_cause.

contributing_factors.description: Conditions that had to hold for the incident to happen and did not cause it alone - a safeguard that did not stop it, a gap in detection or review. A factor held before the incident began: what the response did, declined or left behind - an action taken or not, automatic sync left off - is not one; where it went wrong, say it under went_wrong. Not the root cause again in other words: a factor is something that, had it been otherwise, would have stopped or shortened the incident even with what root_cause says still true. A safeguard the record does not show is one not seen, never one absent: write that no check was seen, not that none ran. An alert finds what its rule watches, not the cause behind it: say a fault was found only by what the record shows found it. Each is answered by at least one action item: one of the record's, named in its addressed_by, or one you propose, whose answers name it.

addressed_by.description: The record's own action items that answer it, by the numbers the record gives them: AI-1. Empty where none of them does. Never an item you propose: that item names, in its own answers, the factors it answers. The record's item that merges this incident's fix answers the fault its own tests cover, never a check missing before the change went out: answer that with an item that puts the check in place for every change like it.

had_it_been_otherwise.description: What would have gone differently had this been otherwise - stopped, shortened or caught sooner - with what root_cause says still true. A factor that only says the root cause again cannot answer this: leave it out of the list.

label.description: CF-1 for the first factor, CF-2 for the next, and so on in the order you give them. Written here and in an item's answers, never in your prose: the reader never sees it.

lessons.description: What went well, what went wrong, and where the incident got lucky - a risk that went unnoticed this time. Any list may be empty. A safeguard the record does not show is one not seen, never one absent: write that no check was seen, not that none ran. How soon the alert came is weighed by the document already, from what was measured: say nothing of it here.

got_lucky.description: Something the record shows went the fortunate way by chance, and would have made it worse had it not. Empty where the record shows none. Not what kind of fault it was, which the impact already says, nor a limit of what the record shows, which is said in assumptions as what was assumed. Not how the service did over a stretch its metrics did not cover, nor what a failure there would have done - the document says how it did.

went_well.description: Where one says how quickly Argus did something, write the span as a working of two instants - a T or P row's instant is its first figure, as T3.1 is T3's: {T3.1 - alert_raised}, not in words ("within seconds"). Set the span beside what it times - the thing its later instant dates - not after something else in the same sentence: "Argus confirmed, {T20.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised, that the rollback had brought the service back", not "Argus confirmed the rollback had brought the service back from the incident's level {T20.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised". Set a purpose or a reason beside the action it belongs to, and say it once. Name what Code-Fix proposed without saying what it does: the action items and Code-Fix's own reading say that, with its conditions.

went_wrong.description: A change the response left in place on purpose, which one of the record's own action items undoes (automatic sync left off), went as designed and did not go wrong; so did what the design leaves to a person - a draft fix to review and merge. Not a limit of what the record shows - logs nobody read, metrics that stop short of the onset: the document says what was read, and anything assumed is said in assumptions. Not the root cause or a contributing factor again - the document says those already.

reaches_a_cause.description: Whether the chain says why the change that set the incident off broke the service, rather than stopping at that change. A step resting on F rows - a reading of the code nothing ran - counts: whether that leaves the cause unverified is cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading's to say. That a new version does worse is what the change did, not why it broke the service: answer false where the chain says the evidence does not show why.

root_cause.description: What caused the incident, in one or two sentences, written for an engineer who was not on the call: the mechanism - why the change that set it off broke the service, as far as the evidence goes, a missing protection or not. Not the trigger, how it was confirmed, what resolved it or what was ruled out - the document states each of those itself. Not one of the contributing_factors: a safeguard that would have stopped it with this mechanism unchanged is said there, not here. What the service did over the stretch the metrics did not watch is not the mechanism: the document says it itself. Whether it was verified the document says itself, from your answer to cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading - do not say it.

still_at_risk.description: What was still at risk at the end of the time Argus held the incident, in one sentence for the same reader - what the fault still in place then could yet do, or the same thing able to happen again. Empty where nothing was. Not whether the service or its metrics were back, nor why - the summary says both. Not what Argus left to a person - a draft fix, automatic sync left off, a recommended action - which the document says itself. Say only what the record says: nothing of the service after that was read.

stops_the_harm.description: One action item, said as the one thing to do: what stops the harm the record shows going on once the action that did not help was put back, and how to confirm at the service that it took effect. Not how long it is kept: the document adds that it stays in place until the fault is fixed. Say only what the record shows. It is listed after your own action items: do not repeat it among them, nor any of the record's own.

symptom.description: What went wrong as somebody using the service saw it, as short as it can be: it is the document's title. One sentence with no number in it, never over 16 words - the thing that went wrong and what happened to it, with an active verb: 'Account pages failed'. Not the metric the alert fired on, not the cause - the document adds the change it began with itself, after your sentence and a 'while', so end on what went wrong, with no clause after it - and not how it was found, which the document's Detection says. Where nobody using the service saw anything wrong, say that and what was seen instead, in that one sentence.
